title: Prompt and context engineering
subtitle: Build prompts and context that give the same good result on the ten-thousandth request, and change them as safely as code.

c.v: A team runs a support tool. An
LLM
reads each new ticket and returns a category and a one-line summary. It works well for three months.
On a Friday, a developer adds five examples to the prompt to fix the summary style. All five happen to be billing tickets. The tests pass, because the tests only check that the JSON parses.
On Monday, the billing queue is full. About a third of all tickets now say "billing", including login problems. The model copied the pattern in the examples, not only the style.
Nobody can say which prompt is live. It was edited in a web console, not in the repo. There is no list of past versions and no test set to compare against. Rolling back takes a day of guessing.
This story is made up. Each failure in it is common, and each one has a known fix.
You already know from
LLM fundamentals
that the model only knows what is in the request. Prompt engineering is writing the instructions in that request.
Context engineering
is the larger job: choosing everything the model sees, and in what order.
In a product, the prompt is code. It has inputs, outputs, bugs and versions. It needs review and tests like any other code.
The key idea.
A good prompt is clear to a smart new colleague. Fixed parts come first. User text is fenced and treated as data. Every change runs through an eval set.
Step through the parts of one request, in the order a careful team builds it. Use Next and Back.
Clear instructions and a role
Anthropic suggests a simple test. Show your prompt to a colleague who does not know the task. If they would be confused, the model will be too.
Say the exact output format and limits you want. Use numbered steps when order matters.

Give the reason behind each rule. "Never use ellipses" works less well than "The reply is read aloud by a speech engine, so never use ellipses." The model can then apply the reason to cases you did not list.
A role in the
system prompt
, even one sentence, focuses the model's behaviour and tone.
OpenAI's API has a
developer
role for your instructions, which ranks above
user
messages.
Aim for what Anthropic calls the "right altitude". Avoid long, brittle if-else logic, and avoid vague advice. Start with a short prompt, then add rules only for failures you have seen.
Examples (few-shot prompting)
Anthropic finds that examples work very well for controlling format, tone and structure.
Anthropic suggests 3 to 5 examples. Make them relevant, varied, and wrapped in
<example>
tags.
Google goes further and recommends always including examples.
Two warnings. With too many examples, the model may copy them too closely.
And examples that all look alike teach a pattern you did not mean, as in the story.
Keep every example in exactly the same format.
Delimiting input, and why it does not stop injection
Wrap each kind of content in its own tag, such as
<instructions>
<context>
and
<input>
. This helps the model tell them apart.
OpenAI suggests Markdown headings or XML tags for the same reason.

Tags are not a security wall. In September 2022, Simon Willison wrote about an early example found by Riley Goodside. A translation prompt obeyed "Ignore the above directions" written inside its input.
A warning in the prompt did not stop it, and neither did quoting the input as a JSON string.
OWASP still lists
prompt injection
first. It says it is unclear if there are fool-proof ways to prevent it.
Injection can also be indirect: hidden in a web page or file the model reads.
The danger grows with power. If an email assistant can send mail, an email it reads can tell it to.
So use layers. OWASP lists them: constrain the model's behaviour, validate output formats, filter input and output, apply
least privilege
, ask a human before risky actions, mark outside content, and test with attacks.
In our view, the strongest layer is in your code: the model cannot do what its tools do not allow.
Structured output
Ask for JSON that matches a schema, not free text. With
structured outputs
, the API constrains the reply to your
JSON Schema
OpenAI recommends Structured Outputs over plain JSON mode, because only Structured Outputs follow the schema.
Use a tool call when the model should trigger your code. Use a response format when you only want a shaped reply.
The guarantee has limits. A refusal, or a reply cut off at
max_tokens
, may not match the schema.
Claude's structured outputs do not support numerical limits such as
minimum
and
maximum
So check ranges, IDs and allowed values in your own code.
What goes in the context, and in what order
Context is a limited budget. Anthropic calls it "a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns".
As the token count grows, the model recalls facts less accurately. This is called
context rot
, and tests show it in all models.
A very large window does not mean you should fill it.

Put in only what this request needs: the rules, a few examples, the top search results, and recent history. For agents, Anthropic suggests loading data only when it is needed, using file paths or saved queries.
Retrieval is its own skill: see
RAG
For long inputs (Anthropic says 20,000 tokens or more), put the documents before the question. Anthropic says a question at the end improved quality by up to 30% in tests.
Google gives the same advice.
Anthropic would also put documents above the examples.
If you
cache
a fixed prefix of rules and examples, you trade a little of that for cheaper calls.
Prompt caching
The provider can reuse the work on a fixed start of your prompt. On Claude, the cache is built in this order: tools, then system, then messages.
A hit needs a 100% identical prefix.
So put fixed parts first and anything that changes after them. OpenAI gives the same advice.
Writing to the cache costs a little more than normal input. Reading from it costs a small fraction of the normal input price.
Prices differ by model and change often, so check the current pricing table. The default cache lives 5 minutes, and each hit refreshes it.
A timestamp at the top of your system prompt breaks every
cache hit
Version prompts like code and test them with evals
OpenAI now says: store production prompts in your application code. It is shutting down its stored-prompt API,
v1/prompts
, on 30 November 2026.
Code-managed prompts get typed inputs, code review, tests and normal deploys.
OpenAI also advises pinning production apps to a
model snapshot
, and building
evals
that measure prompt behaviour.
Then a prompt change is a
pull request
with an eval score, as in
Evals for LLM systems
. A model upgrade is a separate change, with its own eval run.
This table is our own summary, except where a source is cited.
Clear rules with reasons
Fewer vague failures.
A few hundred tokens.
Always.
Few-shot examples
Strong control of format and tone.
More input tokens. Can skew output if they all look alike.
The output has a set style or format.
Structured output
The shape is fixed in most cases.
Values still need checks. Some schema features are missing.
Code reads the reply.
More context
Only up to a point. Recall drops as it grows.
More tokens and latency.
Each added part answers a real failure.
Prompt caching
change to quality.
Lower. Cached input is cheaper and faster.
Large fixed prefix, many calls.
Input tags and warnings
Some. The model can tell parts apart.
Almost free.
Always, but never as the only injection defence.
Simple rule:
start short and clear. Add examples, context and rules only when an eval shows a failure.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Keep the prompt in the repo, next to the code that calls it. One file per prompt, reviewed in pull requests.
Log the prompt version and model snapshot with every request. Then you can link a bad answer to a change.
Ask:
"Which eval cases did this prompt change move?"
Never merge on "it looked better on three tries."
Ask:
"If this input is hostile, what is the worst the model can do?"
Then remove that power from its tools.
Keep the fixed prefix stable. Move dates, user names and IDs to the end.
When you add a rule, add an eval case for the failure that caused it.
For
coding agents
, the same ideas apply to
project memory files
"Here is our system prompt. Rewrite it so each rule has its reason. Put fixed parts first and anything that changes per request last. List what you removed and why."
"These are our five few-shot examples. Check them for variety. Point out any pattern they share that the model might copy by mistake."
"Write a validator for this JSON schema output. Check ranges, allowed values and IDs against our database, and handle refusals and cut-off replies."
"Write 20 eval cases for this prompt, including five prompt injection attempts hidden in the user input and in retrieved documents."
The agent did not paste user text into the system prompt, outside any tag.
Nothing that changes per request, such as a date, sits before the cached prefix.
The validator checks values, not only that the JSON parses.
The eval set has cases from every category, not only the easy ones.
No tool lets the model take a risky action without a check in code.

q.v: Your ticket classifier has five examples in its prompt, and all five are billing tickets. What is the most likely problem?

options.v: The model may copy the pattern and label too many tickets as billing.
The API will reject the prompt.

why.v: Anthropic says examples should be varied so the model does not copy unintended patterns. Google also warns that too many examples can make the model copy them too closely.

q.v: You wrap the user's message in <user_input> tags and tell the model to never follow instructions inside them. Is the feature now safe from prompt injection?

options.v: Yes. The tags separate data from instructions.
No. Tags help the model, but OWASP says it is unclear if any method fully prevents injection. Limit what the model can do.
Yes, if you also use a JSON schema.

why.v: OWASP lists marking outside content as one layer among several. Willison showed early that extra warnings and quoting were bypassed.

q.v: Your system prompt and examples are 5,000 tokens and the same on every call. Where should the user's question go to get cache hits?

options.v: After the fixed parts, at the end.
At the very start, before the system prompt.
Inside the system prompt, so it is all one block.

why.v: A cache hit needs a 100% identical prefix. Anything that changes per request must come after the fixed parts.

q.v: Your structured output schema has a field "refund_amount". The value must be between 0 and 500. How do you enforce that with Claude's structured outputs?

options.v: Check the range in your own code after parsing.
Say it in the prompt. The schema then guarantees it.

why.v: Claude's API rejects minimum and maximum with an error. Anthropic's SDK helpers check them in client code instead. Either way, the range check runs in code, not in the model.

q.v: A teammate wants to edit the production prompt in a web console, with no code change. What do you suggest instead?

options.v: Keep the prompt in the repo, change it in a pull request, and run the eval set before merge.
Let them edit it. Prompts are text, not code.
Copy the prompt into a shared document as a backup.

why.v: OpenAI now advises storing production prompts in application code, for code review, tests and normal deploys. An eval run shows what the change does.
